result: Approximately one-third of dentate gyrus projection neurons labeled during Barnes maze acquisition (33.86%) and enriched environment exposure (27.83%) were semilunar granule cells (SGCs), representing a disproportionate recruitment relative to their ~3-5% population density.
evaluation: All reviewers acknowledge this finding without challenge. Reviewer 1 states 'SGCs account for a third of behaviorally recruited engram neurons, although they represent less than 5% of excitatory neurons in the dentate gyrus' and notes this is 'consistent with previous observations.' The editor describes this as providing 'solid evidence' about distinctive characteristics of recruited neurons.

result: SGCs showed greater sustained firing than GCs with less spike frequency adaptation, and labeled SGCs showed significantly lower adaptation in firing rate than unlabeled SGCs, while labeled and unlabeled GCs did not differ in adaptation ratio.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these intrinsic physiological differences. Reviewer 1 notes 'engram SGCs displayed lower values of adaptation in firing rate than non-recruited SGCs' and states 'Differences in physiology between excitatory neuron subtypes might explain the preferential recruitment of SGCs.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'The sustained firing of semilunar granule cells explained their preferential activation.'

result: There was no difference in resting membrane potential, input resistance, or action potential parameters between labeled and unlabeled GCs, and no cell-type-specific difference in RMP between GCs and SGCs.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings. Reviewer 1 notes that 'SGCs and GCs exhibited numerous differences (e.g., Rin, firing frequency) regardless of whether they were behaviorally activated or not,' implicitly accepting the lack of labeling-dependent differences in basic membrane properties for GCs.

result: No functional glutamatergic synaptic connections were observed between behaviorally labeled SGCs and GCs in 32 paired recordings, and wide-field optogenetic stimulation failed to evoke EPSCs in unlabeled neurons.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises significant concerns about this negative finding, stating 'Without a demonstration that other connections from SGCs (e.g. onto mossy cells or interneurons) are preserved in their preparation and if so at what rates, it is unclear whether this experiment is indicative of the underlying biology or the quality of the preparation.' The reviewer notes that 'even in paired slice recordings from CA3 pyramidal cells the experimentally detected connectivity rates are only around 1%' and that 'The authors would need to record from a lot more than 32 pairs' to make definitive claims. However, the reviewer acknowledges 'The authors now provide evidence that at least some synaptic connections are preserved.'

result: Activation of labeled DG neurons rarely drove inhibitory synaptic currents in unlabeled neurons, with only 1 of 49 SGC-to-GC recordings and 1 of 63 GC-to-SGC recordings showing lateral inhibition, contrasting with robust inhibition observed when activating random cohorts of virally labeled GCs.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 expresses concern that 'optogenetic GC stimulation rarely ever evokes feedback inhibition onto other cells which contrasts with both other in vitro and in vivo studies.' The reviewer notes 'it still remains unclear how the rate of connectivity compares to other studies or a live organism' even after the authors provided control experiments. Reviewer 1 acknowledges the finding but notes the data are 'descriptive and based on correlation rather than causation.' Reviewer 3 states the authors 'provide evidence that lateral inhibition is not playing a role' but also notes 'Exclusive use of slice physiology limits some of these conclusions due to the shearing of connections.'

result: Control experiments showed that focal optical activation of cohorts of GCs labeled with ChR2 based on CAMKII expression supported robust feedback inhibition in the slice preparation, demonstrating that the circuit needed to support lateral inhibition is present.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'The authors now provide evidence that at least some synaptic connections are preserved by recruiting GC assemblies with channelrhodopsin, resulting in feedback inhibition which supports their argument' and 'by stimulating a random subset of granule cells optogenetically.' This addresses the reviewer's concern about preparation quality.

result: Labeled GCs and SGCs received more frequent and larger spontaneous excitatory synaptic inputs than their unlabeled counterparts, suggesting that neurons activated during behavioral experience receive enhanced glutamatergic drive.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding. Reviewer 1 states 'sEPSCs in labeled GCs and SGCs are more frequent and larger than in unlabeled GCs and SGCs, respectively.' Reviewer 3 notes 'The authors report that sEPSCs recorded from labelled sGCS are more frequent, higher in amplitude' as a strength of the study.

result: Labeled neuronal pairs received more temporally correlated spontaneous excitatory synaptic inputs than labeled-unlabeled pairs, with higher peri-occurrence and co-occurrence correlations that could discriminate between L-L and L-U pairs better than chance.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 states 'Probably the most convincing finding in this study is the higher zero-time lag correlation of spontaneous EPSCs in labelled vs. unlabeled pairs' and notes 'The authors now show the baseline EPSC rates and conventional Cross correlograms lending more support to this conclusion.' Reviewer 1 confirms 'the temporal correlation of excitatory events received by pairs of engram neurons was greater than that of pairs of neurons that do not belong to the same ensemble.' Reviewer 3 lists this as a strength: 'temporally correlated than their counterparts.'

result: TTX treatment increased EPSC inter-event interval by twofold, indicating that approximately half the sEPSCs recorded in GCs represent action potential-dependent events.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 initially raised concerns about using spontaneous EPSCs but acknowledges 'The authors now show the baseline EPSC rates and conventional Cross correlograms lending more support to this conclusion,' indicating acceptance of the TTX validation experiment.

result: Mice showed successful Barnes maze learning and enriched environment exposure resulted in significantly more labeled neurons than Barnes maze, with greater context-specific reactivation in EE-exposed mice, though labeling density was sparser than in fear conditioning paradigms.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the behavioral labeling approach. Reviewer 3 notes as a strength that 'The authors confirmed the engram cell properties of activated semilunar granule cells and granule cells in two different paradigms, validating these findings using an enriched environment paradigm.' Reviewer 2 notes the caveat that 'Only about 7% of the engram cells are re-activated one week after exposure' but does not reject the findings.

result: c-Fos co-labeling was observed in less than 10% of tdT-positive neurons after re-exposure, and while the TRAP2 system may miss neurons expressing other IEGs, it remains the best current approach for activity-dependent labeling of DG neurons.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises concern that 'Only about 7% of the engram cells are re-activated one week after exposure, it is unclear how meaningful this assembly is given the high number of cells that may either be labelled unrelated to the EE or no longer be part of the memory-related ensemble.' This questions the validity of the labeled population, though reviewers do not explicitly reject the methodological approach. Reviewer 2 also notes 'one of the biggest caveats of the study is that the ensemble is labelled a full week before the slice experiment.'

result: Behaviorally relevant activation of SGCs and GCs in DG neuronal ensembles is determined by a combination of sustained firing characteristics of SGCs, enhanced glutamatergic inputs, and shared afferent drive rather than by selective circuit-level refinement by recurrent excitation or lateral inhibition.
evaluation: This integrative conclusion receives mixed evaluation. The editor states the study provides 'solid evidence to suggest mechanisms that may be involved in the recruitment of neurons into memory engrams,' but Reviewer 1 notes 'Most of the data presented are descriptive and based on correlation rather than causation.' Reviewer 2's concerns about the negative connectivity findings and Reviewer 3's note that 'Exclusive use of slice physiology limits some of these conclusions' suggest the mechanistic interpretation remains uncertain.
